title: Slack-Free Deep-Unfolded Combinatorial Optimization Solver for Inequality Constraints
authors: Ryo Hagiwara, Shunta Arai, Satoshi Takabe
abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) is used to solve combinatorial optimization problems (COPs). When COPs are implemented on quantum annealers, they are typically encoded as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems, but constraint encodings often increase the number of qubits and the embedding overhead. This issue is particularly important for COPs with inequality constraints, where standard slack-variable formulations introduce additional binary variables. Unbalanced penalization (UP) avoids slack variables, but the original UP formulation requires tuning two penalty coefficients and contains a squared residual term that can increase the number of quadratic couplings. In this paper, we propose the unbalanced penalization Ohzeki method (UPOM), which combines UP with the Ohzeki method for inequality-constrained COPs. UPOM replaces the two static penalty coefficients of original UP with an auxiliary-variable update and removes the squared residual term from the Hamiltonian used for sampling. We further propose the deep-unfolded unbalanced penalization Ohzeki method (DU-UPOM), which learns the step-size schedule of the UPOM update from training instances. Numerical experiments on random knapsack problems show that UPOM improves over original UP and that DU-UPOM reaches optimal solutions in fewer iterations than fixed-step UPOM and other baseline. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework reduces the tuning and embedding burdens of UP while making the Ohzeki method trainable for inequality constraints.
summary: This paper presents DU-UPOM, an advanced solver designed to tackle complex combinatorial optimization problems with inequality constraints for quantum annealers. It improves upon existing methods by combining Unbalanced Penalization with the Ohzeki method and using Deep Unfolding to learn adaptive update schedules. The results show that this learned approach achieves optimal solutions much faster than static or fixed-step alternatives.
main_problem: The core problem is efficiently solving Combinatorial Optimization Problems (COPs) subject to inequality constraints when mapping them onto quantum annealers.
main_result: The proposed Deep-Unfolded Unbalanced Penalization Ohzeki Method (DU-UPOM) significantly improves convergence speed and robustness compared to previous methods by learning the optimal step-size schedule adaptively.
method: The authors combine the Unbalanced Penalization (UP) technique for inequalities with the iterative Ohzeki method, further enhancing it using Deep Unfolding (DU) to train the update step sizes.
model_or_system: The work models COPs as QUBO problems suitable for quantum annealers. The mathematical framework involves penalty functions and iterative sampling updates derived from the Ohzeki transformation.
key_observables: Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the solution relative to the optimum, Optimal Instance Rate (fraction reaching the true optimum), and the learned step-size schedule $\{\eta_t\}$.
important_parameters: Penalty coefficients ($\lambda_1, \lambda_2$), learning rate/step size schedule ($\{\eta_t\}$), and problem instance parameters (e.g., knapsack weights $w_i$ and profits $p_i$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the expectation derivatives required for backpropagation can be estimated accurately from Monte Carlo samples drawn from the sampler distribution.
figures_summary: Figures compare convergence speed (MSE vs. iterations) showing DU-UPOM significantly outperforms fixed-step and baseline methods, and one figure illustrates the nonuniformly learned step-size schedule.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the limitations of standard QUBO encoding for inequalities. It then details UPOM as an improvement over original UP by integrating Ohzeki's method. Finally, it extends this to DU-UPOM, training the update schedule using deep unfolding techniques and validating performance on knapsack problems.
why_interesting: While focused on optimization algorithms rather than fundamental quantum dynamics, the reliance on sampling distributions (MCMC) and the connection to QUBO formulations makes it highly relevant for understanding practical implementations of quantum computation hardware.
